newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe seeks accord to help jobless youth.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe seeks accord to help jobless youth.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged students, and business and trade union leaders on Monday to agree on practical steps to curb "unbearable" 25 percent youth unemployment, a key issue ahead of next year's general election.
France is among those European countries worst hit by unemployment among under 25s, with a jobless rate almost double the 12.7 percent national average, itself a post-war record.

"I hope that all together we can seal today a real accord on a method so that our response to youth employment meets our children's expectations," Juppe said on opening a round-table conference on youth unemployment at his office.

Aware that the anger of 600,000 young people kept waiting at the doors of the consumer society -- and their parents' anxiety -- will weigh heavily in the 1998 poll, President Jacques Chirac has declared a national "crusade" to help them find jobs.

Juppe, who said youth unemployment was unacceptable and a collective failure, insisted participants must explore all possible solutions and be practical rather than yield to a French temptation of grand, wishful statements.
"We need individually tailored steps, rather than some ready-to-wear solution," he said.
Trade unionists were sceptical but agreed concrete steps were what was needed -- "as little blah-blah as possible", said Nicole Notat head of the largest CFDT trade union.

Juppe said his objective was to ease the passage of young people from school or university to work, and break the vicious circle in which employers demand previous work experience from first-time job seekers unable to break into the labour market.
Some 160,000 young people land on a saturated market every year, and the problem will be aggravated when France phases out army conscription in 2002.
Despite demands that the government spend more on job creation, Chirac and Juppe are sticking to budget austerity to qualify France for the single European currency in 1999.

Juppe said the conference, attended by 10 cabinet ministers, would cover boosting apprenticeship, creating flexible contracts opening the labour market to young graduates and helping them look abroad for a first job.
He proposed transferring one billion francs ($190 million) from central to local authorities to help new projects -- "spending less from Paris and more in the field".
The Young Socialists Movement denounced the conference as a vote-grabbing publicity stunt.
Juppe retorted that problems went well beyond the general election and the nation's social cohesion and inventiveness were at stake.
With economic growth prospects brightening, he said he was confident that cuts in working hours and payroll taxes could bring the jobless rate down.

But he ruled out demands by some unions to bring down the retirement age to 55 from 60 to free up jobs for the young, saying it was a short-term solution which would be disastrous as the population grows older.
The talks were likely to rekindle disputes over a proposal by the employers' association CNPF to offer young graduates short-term, low-paid contracts to gain initial work experience.
Unions suspect the bosses of trying to hire low-cost labour, reviving in another form a much-decried proposal for cut-rate wages for young people which triggered student protests in 1994.

Juppe has said he wanted more young people to get their first work experience abroad "because the markets are over there", drawing a rebuke from the Young Socialists that his suggestion was "an amazing acknowledgement of political impotence".
